threads.thread_goal: Align on project scope, roles, and initial mapping of current shelves

messages.text:
Kicking off the Clinic Retail Corner and Supply Shelf Optimisation project for the next three weeks. Goal is to standardise layouts and routines so shelves are safer, easier to work with, and clearer for patients.
First step is mapping what we have now for T1. We will use A1 as the place to capture current vs proposed layouts.
Two asks for everyone:
1) List the shelves and zones you think must be in scope (retail and medical).
2) Share quick pain points you see when stocking or finding items.
Once we have that, we can lock the scope and confirm who keeps A1 up to date.

For scope, I suggest we at least include:
- Front retail corner: over-the-counter meds, vitamins, small food items.
- Treatment room consumables: dressings, syringes, gloves.
- Nurse station cupboard: forms plus some clinical stock.
Pain points I see:
- Similar boxes (dressings, bandages) mixed together.
- Expiry dates hard to see on the back rows.
- Patients sometimes pick up the wrong strength of pain relief from the retail corner.
Happy to start filling in A1 for these areas under T1 once we agree the full list.

Adding a few more shelves I think we should cover:
- Vaccine fridge door racks (for how we place boxes, not the fridge itself).
- Sample collection kits shelf near reception.
- Back room bulk storage for retail top-ups.
Pain points:
- We lose time hunting for specific needle sizes.
- Bulk boxes in the back room are not grouped the same way as the front shelves, so refills are slower.
If we agree these are in scope, I can help with photos and quick notes for T1.

From the retail side, I would include:
- All three gondolas in the waiting area.
- The small impulse shelf by the till.
Pain points I notice when stocking:
- Price labels do not always match what is in the till.
- Some food items with short dates end up hidden behind newer stock.
I am not sure if the impulse shelf by the till should be in scope or separate, so would like guidance there.

For the treatment room, I find it hard to reach some items quickly during busy clinics, especially gloves and alcohol wipes.
Maybe we should include:
- The trolley shelves used during blood draws.
- The cupboard above the sink where we keep disinfectants.
I can help list what is on each of those shelves for T1, but I might need someone to show me how to add it into A1.

On the impulse shelf by the till: I suggest we keep it in scope. It is small, but it is where price mismatches are most visible to patients.
So far, the candidate list is:
- Waiting area gondolas (3)
- Impulse shelf by till
- Front retail corner meds and vitamins
- Treatment room consumables shelves and trolley
- Nurse station cupboard
- Vaccine fridge door racks (layout only)
- Sample kit shelf near reception
- Back room bulk storage for retail
- Disinfectant cupboard above the sink
Anything missing before we freeze this list for the project?
Looks complete to me. Only question: do we treat the nurse station cupboard as one zone or split it into admin vs clinical stock? That might affect how we draw it in A1.

Agree with including all of these. For the nurse station cupboard, I would split into two zones: top shelves for admin, lower shelves for clinical items. That will help later when we design the standard layout under T2.
I am fine with that list. For the back room bulk storage, can we just map the main bays we actually use for retail top-ups, not every single pallet space? That will make T1 easier to finish.

Good point on the nurse station cupboard. Let us treat it as two zones in A1: admin and clinical. For the back room, we will only map the bays used for retail and clinical top-ups, not full storage.
If no one objects by this afternoon, I will consider the scope list closed and record it as our baseline for the project.
No objections from me. The list covers all the places where I struggle to find things during clinics.
Happy with that. Keeping the back room focused on the main bays will help me get T1 done without missing shifts on the shop floor.

Great, closing the scope based on the list in A1: all retail gondolas and impulse shelf, front meds and vitamins, treatment room shelves and trolley, nurse station cupboard (split admin/clinical), vaccine fridge door racks, sample kit shelf, back room top-up bays, and disinfectant cupboard.
That will be our official set of shelves and zones for this project.
On ownership of A1 for T1: I can take the lead on keeping the layout map updated, as I am on site most mornings. Others can send me photos and notes, and I will add them into A1.
Works for me. I can cover photos for the treatment room, nurse station cupboard, and vaccine fridge door racks tomorrow morning and send them over so you can drop them into A1.
I will grab photos and quick notes for the waiting area gondolas, impulse shelf, and back room retail bays on my next late shift and share them for T1.
I can help by listing what is on the trolley shelves and the disinfectant cupboard. I might send it as a simple list so you can place it correctly in A1.

Thanks all. To confirm: 362964 owns updating A1 for T1, with support from the rest of you for photos and notes. Let us aim to have the current layout fully mapped so we can move into T2 design work on the next check-in.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on the new standard shelf layout and zoning

messages.text:
I have uploaded a first draft of the proposed standard layout into A1, based on the mapping from T1. It shows current vs proposed zones for retail and medical shelves.
Can you review the zoning and item groupings, especially for safety and clinical access? We also need to make sure the medical supply layout will work with clinical requirements for T7 and feed into A8 later.

On the retail side in A1, I grouped:
- Pain relief and cold remedies together, with clear separation by strength.
- Vitamins and supplements on a separate bay.
- Food and drink items on the lower shelves, away from clinical-looking products.
For T2, I tried to keep high-demand items at eye level and move anything that could confuse patients (like similar boxes) into clearer blocks. Open to tweaks if something feels off from the shop floor view.

Looking at the retail gondolas in A1:
- I like that pain relief is grouped by strength, but I would swap the mid-strength and high-strength shelves so the strongest products are slightly lower, not right at eye level.
- For the impulse shelf, can we keep only small non-medical items there and move any tablets or sprays back to the main bays? That might reduce confusion.
If we agree, I can adjust the retail zones in A1 under T2.

For the treatment room layout in A1, I see gloves and wipes on the second shelf and syringes on the third. During blood draws, I usually reach for gloves and wipes first, then syringes.
Would it be better to have gloves and wipes together on the top reachable shelf, and syringes just below? I am not sure how that fits with T7, so would like a clinical view.

From a clinical and safety angle for T7 and A8:
- High-risk sharps and controlled items should not be on open trolley shelves. They need to be in closed or locked storage, with only the immediate-use quantity on the trolley.
- Gloves, wipes, and hand gel should be at the most accessible level.
- Dressings and bandages can sit just below.
For the vaccine fridge door racks, we must keep vaccines grouped by type and batch, with clear separation to avoid mix-ups.
I suggest we adjust A1 so the trolley shows only immediate-use items, and the bulk of sharps moves to the locked cupboard zone.

I will update A1 so that:
- Trolley shelves show gloves, wipes, and immediate-use dressings only.
- Syringes and needles move into the locked cupboard zone, with a small clearly marked section for the next patient.
- Vaccine fridge door racks are grouped by vaccine type, with labels for batch separation.
Once that is in, can you confirm it meets T7 requirements so we can capture the notes in A8?

I like the idea of moving the strongest pain relief slightly lower. That should still be easy to find but less prominent.
On the impulse shelf, I agree we should keep it to non-medical items. I will adjust the T2 proposal in A1 so any tablets or sprays move back to the main bays and the impulse shelf is just small accessories and snacks.

Thanks. With that change, the retail layout in A1 looks good to me: clear zones, strongest meds not front and centre, and impulse shelf simplified.
From the shop floor side, I am comfortable using this as the standard layout for retail under T2.

The updated trolley and cupboard layout in A1 makes more sense to me now. Gloves and wipes are where I naturally reach, and the locked cupboard for sharps feels safer.
I do not see any issues for day-to-day blood draws with this setup.

I have reviewed the latest A1 layout for medical supplies against our clinical requirements for T7.
- Sharps and high-risk items are now in locked storage with only immediate-use quantities accessible.
- Gloves, wipes, and hand gel are at optimal reach.
- Vaccine door racks are grouped and separated clearly.
This meets our safety expectations, and I will document the rationale in A8.

On the retail side, with the adjustments you both made in A1 for T2, I am comfortable that the layout is clear for patients and does not encourage self-selection of the strongest meds.
Unless anyone has last-minute concerns, I suggest we approve this as the standard layout for all retail shelves.
No further concerns from me. The retail layout is workable for stocking and clear for customers.
Happy to go ahead with this retail layout as the standard. It should also make stock checks easier once we get to the inspection checklist.
Ok, confirming: the proposed retail layout in A1 under T2 is approved as our standard for the gondolas, impulse shelf, and front meds and vitamins.

For medical supplies, with the locked storage for sharps, clear trolley zones, and vaccine rack grouping now captured in A1 and supported by notes in A8, I am happy to sign off this layout as the standard clinical setup.

threads.thread_goal: Define and finalise rotation, expiry, and inspection procedures

messages.text:
I have drafted a first version of the stock rotation and expiry-check procedure in A2 for T3, plus a basic daily and weekly inspection checklist in A4 for T5.
Can you review the proposed frequencies and checklist items and flag anything missing or unrealistic for your shifts?

In A2, I see:
- Daily visual check for short-dated meds and food.
- Weekly full rotation for all retail and clinical shelves.
- Monthly deep clean and full expiry audit.
For A4, the checklist covers hygiene, stock level, expiry, and labelling.
My only concern is whether a full weekly rotation for all areas is realistic on busy weeks. Maybe we can split zones across days so each area gets a full rotation weekly without one huge task.

From the retail side, a full weekly rotation of all gondolas plus the impulse shelf in one go will be hard on late shifts.
Could we set it so:
- Daily: quick front-facing and check for anything expiring within 2 weeks.
- Twice a week: full rotation for food and drinks.
- Once a week: full rotation for meds and vitamins.
That might be easier to fit around customers.

For clinical shelves, I can manage:
- Daily: quick check of expiry dates for items we open that day (needles, syringes, wipes).
- Weekly: a more detailed check of the trolley and cupboard.
I am not sure how often we should do a full expiry audit on all clinical stock, so I would like guidance there.

From a safety and hygiene perspective for T3:
- Daily: quick expiry and damage check on high-risk items (injectables, controlled meds, short-dated food).
- Weekly: full rotation and expiry check for all clinical shelves and retail meds.
- Twice weekly: rotation for food and drink.
- Monthly: deep clean and full expiry audit for all zones.
We can structure A2 so each shift knows exactly which zones they own on which days, to spread the load.

I will adjust A2 so that:
- Daily: quick check on high-risk and short-dated items.
- Twice weekly: rotation for food and drink.
- Weekly: rotation for meds, vitamins, and clinical shelves.
- Monthly: deep clean and full expiry audit.
I will also add a simple table showing which zones each shift covers on which day, so T3 is clear on responsibilities.

The updated A2 schedule looks workable. Splitting zones by day will help us keep up without blocking patient flow.
For A4, could we mirror that structure so the daily checklist has a short section for each zone, and the weekly one has a tick box for the full rotation and expiry check?

Agree, the new A2 plan is more realistic. For retail, I would like the daily checklist in A4 to include:
- Check front row dates for food and drink.
- Confirm strongest meds are in the correct zone.
- Spot-check 2 random items for price label vs system.
That will help catch issues early.

For clinical checks in A4, could we have:
- Daily: confirm trolley has only in-date items for that day.
- Weekly: check expiry dates on the full trolley and the locked cupboard.
I can follow that easily during clinics.

I have updated A4 for T5 so that:
- Daily checklist: short section per zone (retail, clinical, back room) with quick expiry and label checks.
- Weekly checklist: tick boxes for full rotation and expiry check per zone.
- Monthly section: deep clean and full audit.
I also added the retail-specific items 314783 suggested and the clinical checks 211931 mentioned.

I have reviewed the updated A2 procedure for T3:
- Daily checks focus on high-risk and short-dated items.
- Twice-weekly rotation for food and drink.
- Weekly rotation and expiry check for meds and clinical shelves.
- Monthly deep clean and full audit.
This aligns with our safety expectations and should be manageable across shifts.

The latest A4 version looks clear. The daily checklist is short enough to do between patients, and the weekly one gives a good structure for the full rotation.
I do not see any gaps from the shelf side.
Agreed. The retail parts of A4 match what we can realistically do on shift, and the spot-check for price labels is a good reminder.
The clinical checklist items in A4 are straightforward. I can follow the daily and weekly steps without slowing down clinics.
Given the feedback, I propose we lock in the rotation and expiry-check frequencies in A2 as our standard for each product category and zone.
Also proposing that we approve the current A4 daily and weekly inspection checklist as the version we will use during rollout.

threads.thread_goal: Align labelling, pricing, and training approach before relayout

messages.text:
Ahead of the physical relayout in T6, I have drafted the labelling and pricing guideline in A3 for T4 and a quick-reference training guide in A5 for T8.
We also need to agree how we will run the short training huddles for T9.
Please review A3 and A5 and share any gaps or concerns, especially around how easy they are to follow on shift.

In A3, I like that each label shows product name, strength, price, and expiry visibility rules.
One question: for multi-buy offers, do we have a clear rule on how to show both the single price and the offer price so it still matches the till? I want to avoid confusion at the counter.

Looking at A5, the one-page visual guides per zone are helpful. For the treatment room and trolley, could we add a small box that reminds staff which items must never be moved to the impulse shelf or waiting area (for example, anything that looks like a snack but is actually a supplement)?

For A5, I find the icons easy to follow. I just want to check: will the quick guide be printed and kept near the trolley and cupboard, or only in the staff room? Having it close by would help me during clinics.

On A3, the process for updating prices looks clear, but I want to confirm who will actually do the cross-check with the billing system before we print new labels. That step is key to avoid mismatches.

Good catch on multi-buy offers. I will update A3 so that:
- The main label shows the standard single price.
- A secondary small strip shows the multi-buy offer, using the exact wording from the billing system.
We will also add a step in T4 that any new offer label must be checked with the finance and billing coordinator before printing.
On the cross-check: the finance and billing coordinator will validate any price or offer changes before we print labels. I will add that explicitly into A3 and the T4 workflow so it is not missed.

For A5, I will add a small warning box on the clinical pages listing items that must never be placed in retail or impulse zones.
We will also print the relevant A5 pages and place them near the trolley, cupboard, and retail gondolas, as well as in the staff room.

On training for T9, I suggest we run short 15-minute huddles at the start of each shift for three days:
- Day 1: focus on retail zones and labels.
- Day 2: focus on clinical zones and rotation.
- Day 3: recap and Q and A.
We can use A5 as the main visual and walk people through one real shelf each time.
I like that plan. For late shifts, could we also record a short walkthrough using A5 so anyone who misses a huddle can catch up quickly?
The 15-minute huddles sound manageable between clinics. It would help if the clinical session includes a quick demo of how to use the daily checklist from A4 alongside A5.
Happy to help run the huddles for early shifts and walk through one retail and one clinical shelf using A5 and the A4 checklist.
Good idea. I will add to T9 that we record a short screen and shelf walkthrough using A5, so staff who miss a live huddle can watch it later.
With the multi-buy and cross-check steps added, A3 looks clear from the shop floor side. I am comfortable using it as our reference for labels and prices.
The updated A5 pages with the warning box and printed copies near the zones will make it much easier to follow during busy times.
Given the feedback, I propose we approve A3 as the labelling and pricing guideline for rollout, including the finance cross-check step in T4.

On training, let us confirm the format and dates:
- Three days of 15-minute huddles at the start of each shift next week.
- Use A5 and A4 in each session.
- Record one short walkthrough for anyone who cannot attend.
If everyone is ok with that, we will treat this as the agreed T9 plan.
Works for me. I can cover the mid-shift huddles and help with the recording.
No issues from my side. The timing and format are fine.
I can attend the early clinical-focused huddles. The plan sounds good.
All good from me as well.

Ok, confirming the training format and dates as described: three days of 15-minute huddles per shift next week, using A5 and A4, plus a recorded walkthrough. We will treat this as the agreed T9 approach.

threads.thread_goal: Monitor rollout, capture issues, and agree on follow-up improvements

messages.text:
Rollout week starts today. Shelves are being rearranged under T6 according to the approved layouts in A1, and we are using the final inspection checklist in A4.
Please log any stockouts, misplacements, or expiry issues in A6 for T10, and share quick observations here so we can feed them into the post-rollout review in A7 and T11.

Morning update from the treatment room after the first relayout pass for T6:
- Trolley zones match A1 and are easier to work with.
- Found two boxes of dressings with short dates hidden at the back; logged in A6 as expiry finds.
- No stockouts yet, but I noticed one size of gloves is now slightly further from the main reach point.
I have used A4 to tick off the daily checks.

Retail corner after day one of T6:
- Layout matches A1 for the most part.
- We had one short stockout on a popular cold remedy because I misjudged the new facing space; logged in A6.
- Customers seem to find the vitamins faster.
Using A4, I also spotted one price label that did not match the till and corrected it using A3.

From the clinical side, I had one moment where I reached for syringes on the trolley out of habit, but they are now in the locked cupboard as per A1.
No safety issues, but it slowed me down for a minute. Might be worth highlighting again in the next huddle.
No expiry problems found today; I used A4 to check the trolley.

Thanks for flagging. That is exactly the kind of behaviour change we expected with the new safety setup.
Let us reinforce in the next T9 huddle that sharps are now in the locked cupboard and only immediate-use items should be on the trolley, as per A8.

On the cold remedy stockout logged in A6, we might need to adjust the standard facing count in A1 for that product so the new layout still holds but we carry enough units.
I will review the last week of sales with the store manager before we change anything.

On the glove size that is now further away: I can try swapping that size with a slower-moving one on the same shelf while keeping the overall A1 zone intact. If that works better, we can propose it as a small tweak in T11.
Happy to test a slightly larger facing for that cold remedy. I will monitor over the next two days and keep logging any stockouts or near-misses in A6 for T10.
I will pay extra attention in the next huddle and remind colleagues about the new sharps location. So far, patients have not noticed any delay, but I want to keep it that way.

Quick midweek summary from A6 for T10:
- 1 short stockout on cold remedy.
- 3 expiry finds (all caught before use).
- 2 minor misplacements on the impulse shelf (clinical-looking items moved back).
No major safety incidents. The A4 checklist seems to be helping catch issues early.
Thanks for the summary. From a layout perspective, the only recurring theme I see is the cold remedy facing and the glove size placement. Everything else seems to be one-off corrections.
Agree. The trolley and cupboard layout from A1 is working well after the first day of adjustment. I do not think we need big changes there, just the small glove tweak I mentioned.
On the impulse shelf misplacements, I suspect some staff are still getting used to the new A5 rules. Maybe we can highlight the warning box again in the next T9 recap.
Good point. I will emphasise the A5 warning box in the remaining huddles and in the recorded walkthrough.

As we approach the end of the first full week, I will start drafting the post-rollout review in A7 for T11, using the data from A6 and your comments here.
If you have any final observations on patient flow or appointment impact, please share them so we can also cover T12.

From what I have seen, patient flow in the treatment room is unchanged or slightly better. I do not see any new bottlenecks from the shelf changes.
The only adjustment is remembering the new sharps location, which we are getting used to.

In the waiting area, patients seem to browse less randomly and go straight to the right bay more often. No queues building up around the gondolas.
So from my side, no negative impact on appointment flow.
I will summarise the layout-related issues from A6 into a short list of proposed tweaks for T11: adjust cold remedy facing, swap glove sizes on the shelf, and reinforce impulse shelf rules via A5.
Great, I will incorporate those tweaks into A7 as agreed follow-up actions for T11 and confirm with the store manager that they do not create any new patient flow issues for T12.

To close the loop, confirming that we are keeping the full list of shelves and zones defined earlier in A1 as the ongoing scope for monitoring and improvements. No areas are being dropped from the project.
Also confirming that we are using the final A4 daily and weekly inspection checklist as our standard going forward, with no further changes planned right now.
